lead: This unit explains how a VR scene is built, moved, simulated, organised and drawn fast enough for a headset. After it you can choose a model representation, compose transforms, run basic collision and force steps, manage a VR database, trace the rendering pipeline, and budget LOD, culling and computing power.
about: The unit follows a virtual object from shape to screen. 4.1 gives geometry and appearance; 4.2 places objects with matrices and hierarchies; 4.3 adds collision and forces; 4.4 organises behaviour and the VR database. 4.5 turns the scene into pixels through the graphics pipeline. 4.6 keeps large worlds real-time with level of detail and culling. 4.7 matches the workload to computing architecture. 4.8, taught by only a few universities, covers yaw, pitch, roll and quaternions. Each chapter builds on the previous one: a mesh needs a transform, a transform needs a physics and behaviour layer, and the whole scene must pass through the renderer within a frame budget.

chapters.idea: A virtual object is a shape (geometry) plus a surface description (appearance), and both must be stored before anything can be placed or drawn.
chapters.depth: Geometric modeling and virtual object shape: polygon meshes with vertices, edges, faces and triangles; parametric curves and surfaces; implicit surfaces; voxels and point clouds in outline; normals and tessellation. Object visual appearance: material parameters such as diffuse colour, specular level and roughness; texture images and UV mapping; shaders in outline. Some syllabi call the pair object shape and object visual appearance.

figure.aria: Tree splitting a virtual object into geometry, with mesh and curves, and appearance, with material and texture.

chapters.example: Question: A square wall is stored as two triangles sharing four vertices. Each vertex stores position (3 floats) and UV (2 floats); each float is 4 bytes. Each triangle stores three uint16 indices. The wall material stores diffuse colour as 3 floats. Find the total bytes. Answer: positions 4 × 3 × 4 = 48 B; UV 4 × 2 × 4 = 32 B; indices 2 × 3 × 2 = 12 B; colour 3 × 4 = 12 B; total 48 + 32 + 12 + 12 = 104 B.
chapters.trap: Do not count triangles as vertices; shared vertices use indices. Do not mix float count with byte count, and do not store a whole texture once per vertex.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 components of a VR system; basic 3D coordinates.
chapters.leave: Shader programming and game-engine materials to Unit 5; rotation details to 4.2 and 4.8.

chapters.idea: Every object's world position and orientation comes from multiplying its local transform up through a parent-child hierarchy.
chapters.depth: Kinematics modeling: 4 × 4 homogeneous transformation matrices; translation, rotation and scale; object position; matrix multiplication order with column vectors; object hierarchies and the scene graph; world matrix = parent world × local. Transformation invariants: local distances and child transforms stay fixed inside the parent. Viewing the 3D world and the look-at view matrix in outline, with detail left to 4.5. Some syllabi call this transformation matrices and object hierarchies.

figure.aria: Tree with a world, a base translated to (10,0) and rotated 90 degrees, and an arm at local (2,0).

chapters.example: Question: A robot base sits at (10,0) and is rotated 90° anticlockwise about the z axis. The arm local origin is (2,0). Find the arm world position and orientation. Answer: Rz90 × (2,0) = (0,2); add the base translation: (10,0) + (0,2) = (10,2); orientation is 90°.
chapters.trap: Use parent × local, not local × parent. A parent rotation changes the child position as well as the child axes; matrix multiplication is not commutative.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.1 object vertices; basic vectors and matrices.
chapters.leave: Projection and viewport details to 4.5; quaternion rotation maths to 4.8.

chapters.idea: A physics model detects when objects touch and computes forces that change their motion or surface.
chapters.depth: Physical modeling: collision detection in broad phase and narrow phase; bounding volumes such as sphere, AABB and OBB; contact points and penetration depth; surface deformation with mass-spring or penalty methods; force computation; force smoothing and mapping for haptic output. Keep haptic device hardware and human haptics in Unit 3; here focus on the computation.

figure.title: Collision to force
figure.aria: Flow from two spheres of radius 0.5 metres, distance 0.9 metres, penetration 0.1 metres, spring stiffness 200 newtons per metre, force 20 newtons, to smoothing and response.

chapters.example: Question: Two spheres each of radius 0.5 m have centres 0.9 m apart. A penalty spring with k = 200 N/m acts along the centre line. Find the penetration and the force. Answer: sum of radii = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.0 m; penetration x = 1.0 − 0.9 = 0.1 m; force F = kx = 200 × 0.1 = 20 N along the contact normal.
chapters.trap: Use the sum of both radii, not one radius. Force is a vector along the contact normal; collision detection alone is not a collision response.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.1 geometry; chapter 4.2 transforms for placing bodies.
chapters.leave: Haptic display construction to Unit 3; full rigid-body dynamics to a physics course.

chapters.idea: Behaviour rules make objects react, and model management keeps the growing scene database organised and searchable.
chapters.depth: Behaviour modeling: scripts, state machines, events and simple feedback attached to objects. Model management: VR database, world space and world coordinates, objects, geometry, position and orientation, hierarchy, bounding volume, scripts and attributes, tessellated data, LOD records, cullers and occluders, lights, cameras, 2D controls and control panels, room/stage/area descriptions, world authoring and playback. Mention the VR toolkit only as the container; leave toolkits and game engines to Unit 5.

figure.aria: Stack from world and 4 rooms down to 50 objects per room, 3 LOD geometry records and 2 scripts per object, plus a 2D control panel.

chapters.example: Question: A VR world has 4 rooms, each with 50 objects. Each object has 3 LOD meshes and 2 scripts. Count the mesh records and script records. Answer: objects = 4 × 50 = 200; mesh records = 200 × 3 = 600; script records = 200 × 2 = 400.
chapters.trap: A script belongs to the object, not to every LOD. Multiply records by object instances; do not multiply by rooms alone and forget objects.
chapters.leave: Scene-graph APIs and C# scripting to Unit 5; culling selection to 4.6.

chapters.idea: The rendering pipeline turns 3D model coordinates into 2D pixels through a fixed order of transforms and raster steps.
chapters.depth: Graphics and rendering pipeline: model, world, view (look-at), projection, clipping, normalised device coordinates, viewport, rasterisation and fragment shading. Canonical view and perspective transform; viewport transform; lights and cameras. Mention two-eye rendering for stereo, with display technology left to Unit 3 and culling left to 4.6. Some syllabi call this the graphics pipeline and transformations.

figure.title: Rendering pipeline
figure.aria: Pipeline from model and world transforms through camera view, perspective projection, clipping and viewport mapping to raster and shading.

chapters.example: Question: A point in camera space is (2,1,4). A pinhole camera has focal length f = 2. Find its image-plane coordinates before viewport mapping. Answer: x′ = f x / z = 2 × 2 / 4 = 1; y′ = f y / z = 2 × 1 / 4 = 0.5; image point = (1,0.5).
chapters.trap: Do not drop the perspective divide by z or w. Clip before viewport mapping; viewport mapping changes pixels, not the 3D position.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.2 transformation matrices; chapter 4.1 mesh data.
chapters.leave: Stereo display hardware to Unit 3; LOD and culling to 4.6.

chapters.idea: Real-time VR draws only what is visible and only at the detail needed, so large worlds stay inside the frame budget.
chapters.depth: Level of detail, culling and large environments: discrete and continuous LOD chosen by distance or screen size; view-frustum culling, backface culling, occlusion culling, cells and portals, occluders; real-time rendering of large-scale environments; tessellated data and LOD records managed as in 4.4. Some syllabi call this management of large-scale environments and real-time rendering.

figure.title: Culling and LOD
figure.aria: Flow from 10,000 objects through frustum culling to 30 percent, occlusion culling to 50 percent, 1,500 visible objects, LOD to 40 percent, and 600,000 triangles.

chapters.example: Question: A scene has 10,000 objects, each with 1,000 triangles. Frustum culling keeps 30%, occlusion culling keeps 50% of those, and LOD keeps 40% of triangles. Find visible objects and rendered triangles. Answer: objects = 10,000 × 0.30 × 0.50 = 1,500; triangles = 1,500 × 1,000 × 0.40 = 600,000.
chapters.trap: Multiply culling fractions; do not add percentages. LOD reduces triangles, not object count, and occlusion culling needs real occluders.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.4 model records and LODs; chapter 4.5 pipeline.
chapters.leave: Hardware parallel processing to 4.7; scene-graph implementation to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: VR needs a computing architecture with enough parallel work and low enough latency to deliver frames on time.
chapters.depth: Computing architectures for VR: workstation-based systems, distributed systems and parallel processing for real-time VR; CPU scene update and GPU rendering split; frame budget and motion-to-photon latency in outline. Keep display types and optics in Unit 3 and tracking hardware in Unit 2.

figure.title: Latency chain
figure.aria: Serial latency chain of 2 milliseconds tracking, 3 milliseconds CPU update, 5 milliseconds GPU render and 2 milliseconds display, giving 12 milliseconds total, which exceeds an 11.1 millisecond 90 hertz budget.

chapters.example: Question: A VR system targets 90 frames per second. One frame takes 2 ms tracking, 3 ms CPU update, 5 ms GPU render and 2 ms display. Does it meet the budget, and what is its maximum frame rate? Answer: budget = 1000 / 90 = 11.1 ms; actual = 2 + 3 + 5 + 2 = 12 ms; it misses the budget; maximum rate = 1000 / 12 = 83.3 frames per second.
chapters.trap: Use the same unit for every latency. 90 Hz allows about 11.1 ms per frame, not 90 ms. Parallelism can shorten some stages but not the display refresh.
chapters.leave: Headset display optics to Unit 3; tracker hardware to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Orientation can be written as yaw, pitch and roll or as a unit quaternion, which avoids gimbal lock.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. 3D rotations: yaw about the vertical axis, pitch about the side axis, roll about the forward axis; Euler order; gimbal lock; axis-angle representation; quaternions q = w + xi + yj + zk, unit quaternion, half-angle form q = (cos θ/2, sin θ/2 · axis); multiplication order; inverse as conjugate; conversion to a rotation matrix and to yaw-pitch-roll in outline.

figure.aria: Tree of orientation representations: Euler angles split into yaw, pitch and roll, plus axis-angle, quaternion and matrix.

chapters.example: Question: Rotate the point (1,0,0) by 90° about the z axis. Write the quaternion and the result. Answer: θ/2 = 45°; q = (cos 45°, 0, 0, sin 45°) = (0.7071, 0, 0, 0.7071); the rotated point is (0,1,0).
chapters.trap: Use the half angle, not the full angle. Normalise the quaternion, and remember quaternion multiplication is not commutative; Euler order changes the final orientation.
chapters.leave: Full rigid-body rotation proofs to a maths course; tracker orientation hardware to Unit 2.
